If you've ever worked retail you know the feeling. One week the store is dead and the next week everyone needs a winter coat. Stores kind of have to guess what's coming and clothes especially change with the seasons. Nobody is buying a heavy puffer coat in July. I wanted to see if that actually shows up in real sales numbers and whether the weather has anything to do with it.

## The Dataset

I combined two sources monthly retail sales from the Census Bureau and monthly weather for Salt Lake City from Open-Meteo. I picked Salt Lake because it actually has real seasons. Each row is one month for one store type from January 2016 to December 2025. Sales are in millions of dollars.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")

month_names = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
               "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]

retail = pd.read_csv("data/processed/retail_weather.csv")

retail["seasonal_index"] = retail["sales_millions"] / retail.groupby(
    ["category", "year"])["sales_millions"].transform("mean")

no_2020 = retail.loc[retail["year"] != 2020].copy()

print("Rows:", len(retail))
print("Columns:", retail.shape[1])
print("Store categories:", retail["category"].nunique())
```

**What we see:** The dataset has 600 total rows covering 5 store types across 120 months each so there are no missing months. The store types are all completely different sizes. Food and beverage is by far the biggest averaging around $71.1 billion a month with general merchandise right behind it at about $67.6 billion. Building materials sits in the middle around $36.8 billion and clothing comes in around $21.9 billion. Sporting goods is the smallest at roughly $7.2 billion a month. That is exactly why I went with the seasonal index because graphing raw dollar amounts would make the smaller stores look totally flat.

### Salt Lake City's climate

```{python}
weather = retail.drop_duplicates(["year", "month"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 8))

sns.lineplot(
    data=weather,
    x="month",
    y="avg_temp_f",
    marker="o",
    color="firebrick",
    ax=axes[0],
)

axes[0].set_xticks(range(1, 13), labels=[])

axes[0].set(
    xlabel="",
    ylabel="Average temperature (°F)",
    title="Temperature by month",
)


sns.barplot(
    data=weather,
    x="month",
    y="total_precip_in",
    color="lightsteelblue",
    errorbar=None, 
    ax=axes[1],
)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(1, 13), labels=month_names)  
axes[1].set(
    xlabel="",
    ylabel="Total precipitation (inches)",
    title="Precipitation by month",
)

fig.suptitle("Salt Lake City climate, 2016-2025")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


**What we see:** Salt Lake has really clear seasons. It's hottest in July about 82F on average and coldest in January about 30F It's wettest in March about 3.4 inches with April next and then it dries out a ton over the summer july only gets about 0.16 inches the light band around the temperature line shows how much each month changes from year to year.

## Monthly Seasonality

**Question:** Do different kinds of stores peak in different months?

```{python}
 # Monthly Seasonality Plot
season = no_2020.groupby(["category", "month"])["seasonal_index"].mean().reset_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.5))
sns.lineplot(
    data=season, 
    x="month", 
    y="seasonal_index", 
    hue="category", 
    marker="o", 
    ax=ax
)
ax.axhline(1.0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), labels=month_names)
ax.set(
    xlabel="", 
    ylabel="Seasonal index (1.0 = average month)", 
    title="Average seasonal pattern by store type (2020 excluded)"
)
ax.legend(title=None, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.08), ncol=2)
plt.show()
```


**What we see:** Every store type has its own rhythm clothing swings the most. Its best month is December index of 1.56 and its worst is January so the average December is about 2.2 times bigger than the average January sporting goods is next at about 1. 85 times Building materials peaks in May and bottoms out in February which is the spring peak I guessed. In 2016 alone it went from about $21.3 billion in January to about $33.4 billion in May. Food and beverage is the flattest at about 1.22 times which makes sense since people buy groceries no matter what season it is It still gets about a 10% bump in December though The holiday season shows up for the other store types too mostly in December. Clothing sporting goods and general merchandise all peak then and November is a smaller bump of about 8% to 13%.

## What Did 2020 Do?

```{python}
sales_by_year = retail.pivot_table(index=["category", "month"], columns="year",
                                   values="sales_millions")
change_2020 = ((sales_by_year[2020] / sales_by_year[2019] - 1) * 100).rename("pct_change").reset_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
sns.lineplot(data=change_2020, x="month", y="pct_change", hue="category",
             marker="o", ax=ax)
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), labels=month_names)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="2020 sales vs. same month in 2019 (%)",
       title="The 2020 shock by store type")
ax.legend(title=None, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.08), ncol=2)
plt.show()
```

**What we see:** 2020 really messed up normal patterns but clothing got hit the hardest dropping 88% in April down to just $2.5 billion sporting goods was the next worst, dropping 45% in April before bouncing back fast by June. On the flip side food and beverage and building materials never dropped below 2019 levels as people stocked up on groceries and started DIY projects at home general merchandise stayed surprisingly steady, while clothing remained the slowest to recover through the end of the year.

## Key Findings

1. **Seasonality:** Clothing is the most seasonal store type (December is about 2.2 times January) and sporting goods is next. Food and beverage is the flattest at about 1.22 times. Building materials peaks in May and most of the others peak in December.
2. **Weather:** Building materials looks strongly tied to temperature at first (0.62), but once the calendar is removed all the adjusted correlations are weak (about -0.14 to 0.21). So weather doesn't explain much beyond the normal seasons.
3. **2020:** Clothing took the deepest hit with an 88% drop in April 2020, while food and beverage, building materials, and general merchandise held steady or grew.

## Limitations

- Sales data is national, but the weather data is only from Salt Lake City.
- Census estimates get revised over time I got this data retrieved 2026-11-05)
- Open Meteo weather numbers are reanalysis models not direct weather station readings.
- 2020 was left out of the seasonality and weather sections because it was such an unusual year.
